Rethinking Birthright Citizenship: A Call for Reform

The following is a rhetorical exercise presenting arguments made by advocates of this position.

Ladies and gentlemen,

We gather today to discuss something fundamental — the meaning of American citizenship itself.

The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in 1868 for a profound and righteous purpose: to guarantee that formerly enslaved Americans and their children could never be denied their birthright as citizens of this nation. That cause was just. That cause was noble. And nothing I say here today diminishes that history.

But I stand before you to argue that the modern interpretation of that amendment has drifted far from its original intent — and that this drift carries real consequences we can no longer afford to ignore.

The Question of Intent

Senator Jacob Howard, who authored the citizenship clause, explicitly stated it would "not, of course, include persons born in the United States who are foreigners." The phrase "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" was not decorative language. It was a deliberate qualification. Yet over time, through practice rather than through any definitive Supreme Court ruling addressing unauthorized immigration specifically, we have arrived at an interpretation the framers of that amendment would scarcely recognize.

The Reality We Face

Today, the United States stands nearly alone among developed nations in granting automatic citizenship based solely on geographic location of birth. Canada is our only peer in the developed world maintaining this policy. The United Kingdom ended it in 1983. Australia ended it in 1986. France, Germany, Italy, Japan — virtually every nation we compare ourselves to has recognized that citizenship must be tied to something more substantive than coordinates on a map.

Are all of these nations heartless? Are they unjust? Or have they simply recognized a common-sense principle — that citizenship in a modern nation represents a covenant, a mutual bond of allegiance and obligation, not an automatic transaction?

The Incentive Structure

We must be honest about what the current system creates. When citizenship — the most valuable legal status our nation can confer — is granted automatically to anyone born on our soil regardless of their parents' legal status, we create a powerful incentive structure that undermines the legal immigration system.

Every year, thousands of expectant mothers travel to the United States specifically to give birth on American soil. This is not speculation — it is a documented, commercialized industry. "Birth tourism" agencies openly advertise packages promising American citizenship for newborns. They market the benefits: access to American public education, eventual sponsorship of family members, a passport that opens doors worldwide.

And for those who cross our borders without authorization, the birth of a child on American soil creates an immediate anchor — a connection that complicates enforcement, that adds layers of legal and humanitarian complexity to every immigration proceeding, and that makes the already difficult task of maintaining an orderly system exponentially harder.

I want to be clear: I do not blame any parent for wanting the best for their child. That impulse is universal and human. But our policy should not be designed to reward circumvention of the law. Our compassion should not be a tool for exploitation.

What Citizenship Should Mean

American citizenship is not a mere document. It is not a coupon to be clipped. It is a sacred bond — a promise between an individual and a nation, carrying duties as profound as its privileges.

The citizen votes. The citizen serves on juries. The citizen may be called to defend this nation in arms. The citizen pays taxes and participates in self-governance. Citizenship is — or should be — an act of mutual commitment.

When we cheapen the means by which citizenship is acquired, we cheapen citizenship itself. When it can be obtained through a plane ticket and fortunate timing, we tell every immigrant who spent years navigating the legal process, who studied our history, who swore an oath of allegiance with tears in their eyes, that their sacrifice and commitment were unnecessary. That the front door and the back door lead to the same destination.

That is not fairness. That is an insult to legal immigrants everywhere.

The National Security Dimension

We live in an age of unprecedented global mobility. The framers of the Fourteenth Amendment could not have conceived of a world in which a person could fly from any nation on Earth to the United States in under twenty-four hours, give birth, and return home with an American citizen in hand.

Automatic birthright citizenship, as currently interpreted, means we have effectively no control over who becomes an American. A child born to parents with no allegiance to this country, no intention of residing here, no connection to our communities or our values — that child is, by current practice, as fully American as the sons and daughters of families who have built this nation for generations.

This is not a question of ethnicity. This is not a question of race. This is a question of whether a nation has the sovereign right — indeed, the sovereign obligation — to determine the terms of membership in its own political community.

Every nation on Earth claims that right. It is time we exercised ours responsibly.

A Proposal for Reform

What I advocate is not radical. It is not extreme. It is the international norm.

I propose that citizenship at birth be granted to children born in the United States who have at least one parent who is a United States citizen or lawful permanent resident. This is the standard used by most of the democratic world. It maintains America's generous and welcoming character while ensuring that citizenship reflects a genuine connection to this country.

Children born to unauthorized immigrants would not be stateless — they would hold the citizenship of their parents, as is the case in most nations. And nothing would prevent those children from eventually pursuing American citizenship through the legal channels available to all who wish to join our national family.

This reform could be pursued through constitutional amendment — the most thorough approach — or through legislative action testing the boundaries of the current interpretation, bringing the question before the Supreme Court for definitive resolution.

Answering the Critics

I know the objections. I have heard them, and I take them seriously.

Some will say this is motivated by nativism or racial animus. I reject that categorically. This proposal applies equally to every person of every race, ethnicity, and national origin. A child born to unauthorized Canadian immigrants would be treated identically to a child born to unauthorized Mexican immigrants. This is about legal status, not identity.

Some will say we would create a class of stateless children. This is incorrect. International law and the laws of nearly every nation provide citizenship through parentage. The children affected would hold the citizenship of their parents.

Some will say this would be too difficult to administer. Yet somehow, nearly every other developed nation manages it. Are we saying America — the nation that put men on the moon and built the greatest system of self-governance in human history — cannot manage what Germany and Australia handle routinely?

Some will say the Fourteenth Amendment is settled law. But constitutional interpretation has evolved before. The Supreme Court has reversed itself when prior interpretations proved unworkable or unjust. The question of birthright citizenship as applied to unauthorized immigrants has never been squarely addressed by the Court. It is time for that clarity.

The Deeper Principle

At its core, this debate is about what kind of nation we wish to be.

I believe in immigration. I believe America is enriched by those who come here seeking freedom and opportunity. I believe the immigrant story is the American story.

But I also believe that immigration must be orderly. It must be lawful. It must reflect the consent of the governed. And it must not be driven by loopholes and perverse incentives that undermine the very system designed to welcome newcomers fairly and sustainably.

A nation that cannot define its own membership cannot long endure as a nation. A citizenship that means everything to those who earn it must not mean nothing in how it is granted.

A Call to Action

I call upon my fellow Americans — native-born and naturalized alike — to join this conversation with open hearts and clear minds. Set aside the reflexive accusations. Set aside the partisan noise. Ask yourselves honestly:

Does it make sense that the most powerful citizenship on Earth is granted more carelessly than a driver's license?

Does it serve justice that those who follow the rules wait years while those who circumvent them can secure citizenship for their children overnight?

Does it honor our immigrant heritage to maintain a system that incentivizes illegal entry over legal application?

The answer, I believe, is no.

Let us reform our citizenship laws not out of fear, but out of reverence — reverence for what American citizenship means, for the generations who fought and bled and sacrificed to make it valuable, and for the future Americans who deserve a system worthy of the nation they will inherit.

American citizenship should be a treasure, earned and cherished — not an accident of geography.

Thank you, and God bless the United States of America.

We must confront the reality that birthright citizenship has become a powerful incentive for illegal immigration. Our nation's future depends on our willingness to make tough but necessary decisions to preserve the core of what makes America exceptional. Repealing birthright citizenship is not about turning away from our heritage as a nation of immigrants; it is about ensuring that the path to citizenship is lawful, fair, and respected.

Let us come together to protect the integrity of American citizenship.
